name: Opportunity rover (MER-B)

location.name: Perseverance Valley, western rim of Endeavour crater, Meridiani Planum

headline: Built for 90 days, it drove a marathon across Mars in 14 years, until dust hid the Sun
story: Early on 25 January 2004, Universal Time, Opportunity bounced to a stop on its airbags in Meridiani Planum, inside a small crater later named Eagle. It was built to work for 90 Martian days and drive about 1,000 meters. Right at its landing site it found hematite, a mineral that forms in water.

It kept going for more than 14 years. In July 2014 it passed the 39 kilometers driven on the Moon by the Soviet Lunokhod 2, setting the off-world driving record, and in March 2015 its odometer passed the length of a marathon. On the rim of Endeavour crater it found strong signs of ancient water much like a drinkable lake on Earth.

In June 2018 a dust storm wrapped the whole planet and blotted out the Sun the solar-powered rover lived on. Its last signal arrived on 10 June. More than a thousand recovery commands went unanswered, and NASA declared the mission over on 13 February 2019. Opportunity rests in Perseverance Valley, a shallow gully on the inner slope of Endeavour's western rim, where HiRISE has photographed it from orbit.

facts.label: Planned mission
facts.value: 90 sols and about 1,000 meters of driving

facts.label: Mission ended
facts.value: 13 February 2019, after its last signal on 10 June 2018 (sol 5,111)

images.caption: Opportunity's last panorama, 354 frames taken from 13 May to 10 June 2018 at its final spot in Perseverance Valley. Its tracks descend from Endeavour's rim on the horizon.
Seen by HiRISE on 20 September 2018, as the dust storm cleared: Opportunity is the small blip at the center of this view of Perseverance Valley.
The last image Opportunity sent home, on 10 June 2018: a dark, noisy Pancam frame aimed at a Sun hidden by dust. The transmission stopped before the frame was complete.
